summary: Design Y is slightly stronger overall: it gives a more testable safety and pacing plan for the chosen race, while Design X is cleaner and less over-designed. Both fit the brief well and preserve the same core race structure.

differences.aspect: Safety specification for six simultaneous MR players
differences.design_x: Design X’s prototype decision specifies fast walking, 1.2 m clearance, and hazards at least 0.6 m from the edge. Its final layout repeats these constraints, but does not explicitly separate six start positions or protect venue doors.
differences.design_y: Design Y’s prototype adds separated starts, no lane-cutting, no running, and no upward-looking tasks while moving. Its final build plan also requires all four doors to stay clear, lanes never to cross, 1.2 m corridors, and 0.6 m wall clearance.
differences.evidence: Prototype Decisions: Design X, “เว้นทาง 1.2 เมตร” and hazards “ห่างขอบอย่างน้อย 0.6 เมตร”; Design Y, “แยกจุดเริ่ม 6 คน ห้ามตัดเลนหรือวิ่ง” and “ไม่มีภารกิจที่ต้องเงยหน้าขณะเดินเร็ว.” Final Build Plan: Design Y explicitly keeps “four real doors completely clear.”

differences.design_x: Design X has seven ordered checkpoints and a straightforward escalation, but its Prototype Flow only broadly says hazards become harder from 1:30 onward. It does not identify an explicit first safe teaching encounter.
differences.design_y: Design Y deliberately teaches dodging with a sparse hazard set between checkpoints 1–2, escalates hazards through checkpoints 4–6, provides a hazard-free recovery point at checkpoint 7, then puts two distinct final hazard groups before the finish.
differences.evidence: Design Y Final Build Plan specifies an “easy-to-read hazard set between checkpoints 1–2,” gradual density from 4–6, “checkpoint 7... calm and hazard-free,” and two final hazard groups between 8–9. Design X Prototype Flow says at 1:30 that hazards “start to require more timing,” without comparable onboarding detail.

differences.aspect: Scope and risk of overloading a short race
differences.design_x: Design X uses seven checkpoints, two hazard moments, and a simple city-race premise. That is compact for a five-minute rematchable race.
differences.design_y: Design Y uses nine checkpoints, a story turn, dense middle hazards, a scenic pause, and a two-group bridge climax. This creates stronger authored pacing, but may be more content than necessary for a five-minute competitive run.
differences.evidence: Prototype Plans: Design X Decision, “7 checkpoints in order”; Design Y Decision, “two long lanes, 9 checkpoints.” Design Y Flow includes the checkpoint-7 scenic pause at 3:15 before the 3:45 final sequence.

differences.aspect: Consistency and clarity of the physical route
differences.design_x: Design X initially describes “two long lanes,” while its Prototype Sketch shows one winding route. Its final plan resolves this partly as a two-lane-style out-and-back route, but the shift makes the playable footprint less immediately clear.
differences.design_y: Design Y also shows one route in the sketch despite calling for two lanes, but its final plan explicitly says the two gently bending lanes span the court and “must never cross,” alongside six separated spawn positions.
differences.evidence: Design X Options: “two long lanes”; Design X Prototype Sketch: one path polyline; Design X Final Build Plan: “two-lane-style zigzag route.” Design Y Prototype Sketch likewise has one path, while its Final Build Plan adds “lanes must never cross” and “six separated spawn positions.”

differences.design_x: Design X’s sword-combat option says all six can play in separated zones, while acknowledging that swinging and dodging require careful spacing.
differences.design_y: Design Y’s sword-combat option explicitly says that if safe personal space is insufficient, the group should be reduced to 2–3 players per round. That is less aligned with the six-person brief, but more candid about real-space safety.
differences.evidence: Three Options, battle option: Design X says “six players simultaneously in separate zones”; Design Y says “if packed too tightly, reduce to 2–3 people per round.”

why: Design Y gives the builder clearer controls for shared-space safety and a more deliberate learn-escalate-climax sequence. Design X’s smaller seven-checkpoint structure is a genuine advantage for feasibility and replayability, but its route representation is less consistent and its safety plan is less operationally specific.
x_weaknesses: The prototype sketch does not clearly depict the promised two-lane route.
It lacks explicit separated spawn positions and door-clearance requirements.
Its difficulty ramp is less concretely teachable in the first minute.
y_weaknesses: Nine checkpoints plus narrative beats may make a five-minute race feel busy.
The deliberately visually narrow final bridge could make some players over-focus on foot placement, even though the plan preserves a 1.2 m corridor.
Its sketch still does not visibly show both promised lanes.
improvements: For Design X, revise the prototype sketch to show both physical lanes, six spawn positions, spectator boundary, doors, and the 1.2 m safe corridors.
For Design Y, consider combining one or two middle checkpoints so the race retains its teaching ramp without diluting competitive momentum.
For both Design X and Design Y, run a six-player walking-speed test to confirm that reset-to-last-checkpoint penalties do not leave early-failing players unable to meaningfully finish.
